Rural populations in Mecklenburg County, representing approximately 3.2% of the county's total population, face distinct challenges in maternal healthcare despite the county's overall urban character. These rural communities, primarily located in the northern and southern peripheries of the county, experience significant disparities in pregnancy outcomes compared to their urban counterparts. Limited healthcare infrastructure, with only two obstetric practices serving rural areas, creates geographical barriers where residents must travel an average of 18.7 miles to access specialized prenatal care. Transportation challenges are exacerbated by inconsistent public transit coverage, with 38% of rural residents lacking reliable transportation to medical appointments. Additionally, socioeconomic factors compound these access issues, as rural residents experience higher rates of uninsurance (17.3% vs. 11.8% urban) and lower median household incomes ($47,200 vs. $68,300). These structural barriers contribute to delayed prenatal care initiation, reduced visit frequency, and ultimately poorer pregnancy outcomes among rural residents. This summary examines the epidemiological profile of pregnancy-related health outcomes in rural Mecklenburg County populations to highlight these disparities and inform targeted interventions.
